\section{Introduction}
Passive Optical Network (PON) is widely deployed in FTTx access networks~\cite{} and in cellular (LTE, 5G) X-haul networks~\cite{}.
Given popular deployment of PON, protecting user traffic confidentiality in PON is essential. 
However, major PON protocols standardized by ITU-T and IEEE support only payload encryption, not header encryption. Recent studies suggest that the resulting plaintext headers can be exploited to infer user activity~\cite{PLI}.


In this paper, we propose \textbf{SecurePON}, a security-enhanced PON architecture that randomizes the XGEM Port-ID to prevent an adversary on the splitter from tracking per-ONU traffic, while preserving the framing and multiplexing functions on which ONUs depend.

\section{Background}

\subsection{PON Topology}

In a major PON architecture~\cite{itu-g9843,itu-XGPON,itu-XGSPON,itu-NGPON2,itu-50GPON}, an Optical Line Terminal (OLT), located at the Central Office (C.O.), is connected to multiple Optical Network Units/Optical Network Terminals (ONUs/ONTs) through a passive splitter. ONUs and ONTs are basically the same; an ONU is typically installed at an enterprise or MDU to serve FTTB/FTTN services, while an ONT is typically installed at home to serve FTTH service. ONU is typically called a "Fiber Optic Modem".

\textbf{Downstream Traffic (OLT $\rightarrow$ ONU/ONT)} is broadcast over the passive splitter. 


\textbf{Upstream Traffic (ONU/ONT $\rightarrow$ OLT)} is TDMA based, where each ONU/ONT transmits in its assigned time slot~\cite{novelapon}. 

Because downstream traffic is broadcast through the splitter, an ONU/ONT can passively observe traffic destined for any ONU/ONT sharing the same splitter.





\section{Threat Model}
Current PON specifications from ITU-T and IEEE define a limited threat model that considers only payload leakage to an adversary due to its broadcast characteristics~\cite{itu-g9843,itu-XGPON,itu-XGSPON,itu-NGPON2,itu-50GPON}. As a result, the payload is encrypted, but the header remains in plaintext. (Table 1)

The three encapsulation methods (GEM, XGEM, Ethernet) expose different fields in plaintext to an adversary 
sharing the splitter. 
\textbf{GEM} carries a 12-bit PLI that reveals payload length, and a 12-bit Port-ID that identifies the ONU. 
\textbf{XGEM} carries a 14-bit PLI that reveals payload length , and a 16-bit Port-ID that identifies the ONU. 
\textbf{Ethernet} has the 16-bit Length/Type field that reveals payload length when in length-mode, and the 15-bit LLID identifies the ONU.

Each frame's header contains payload length information. Recent studies show that such payload length information could be exploited to infer user's traffic which means an adversary who shares same splitter as victim can leak user traffic by just receiving optical signals from same splitter and there is no neccessity for an adversary to install in-line optical tap because all downstream traffic is broadcast over PON~\cite{PLI}.
